title: France's riots: revolution without utopia
gist: France's current riots began as high-school strikes over run-down lycées in the banlieues of Créteil and Saint-Denis. According to the government, they escalated through La France Insoumise interventions amplified on social media, and they have turned into unusually violent vandalism with anti-French symbolism. Zagha argues that, unlike May 68 or the gilets jaunes, the unrest lacks a utopian project and reflects a 'décivilisation' and deep integration fractures in contemporary France.

insights.claim: France's current riots began as strikes by high-school students at run-down lycées in Créteil and Saint-Denis protesting dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classes and too few teachers.
insights.so_what: Underinvestment in public services in deprived suburbs can quickly become a source of national instability.
insights.quote: high-school students went on strike to protest against the insalubrious state of the buildings, overcrowding in classes and insufficient numbers of teachers
insights.locator: Today, whenever French university and high-school
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha

insights.claim: The French government says the school protests were exploited and inflamed by MPs from Jean-Luc Mélenchon's La France Insoumise, whose interventions spread on social media and encouraged copycat blockades across France, including wealthy Paris neighbourhoods.
insights.so_what: Far-left political amplification through social media raises French political risk and polarisation ahead of elections.
insights.quote: Within days, the government says, the situation had been exploited and inflamed by the interventions of MPs from La France Insoumise
insights.locator: Today, whenever French university and high-school
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha

insights.claim: The original education protest has been overtaken by uncontrolled rioting infiltrated by casseurs, violent vandals often not enrolled at the schools they target.
insights.so_what: Once protests are taken over by vandals, meeting their stated demands is less likely to end the unrest.
insights.locator: The original protest, demanding better teaching
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha

insights.claim: Zagha says the deliberate violence in the current French riots is more unsettling than in May 68 or the gilets jaunes: a headteacher in Marseille was doused in petrol and an undercover officer in Belfort was kicked in the head while unconscious.
insights.so_what: An escalation in protest violence raises security costs and could hurt France's appeal for tourism and investment.
insights.quote: the current level of deliberate physical violence and wanton vandalism has been unsettling
insights.locator: The original protest, demanding better teaching
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha

insights.claim: An arson attack damaged Nantes' Lycée Nelson Mandela, an eco-friendly school built in 2014 at a cost of €54m.
insights.so_what: Destruction of public infrastructure adds fiscal costs for a French state already under budget strain.
insights.quote: An arson attack at the Lycée Nelson Mandela in Nantes caused extensive damage to the eco-friendly school, which was built at a cost of €54m (£46m) in 2014.
insights.locator: The original protest, demanding better teaching
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha

insights.claim: A new feature of French unrest is open anti-French sentiment: some rioters from deprived suburbs wrap themselves in Algerian and Moroccan flags and voice support for Palestine, which the author links to Islamist propaganda and failed cultural integration of French-born youth.
insights.so_what: Integration tensions feed right-wing populist momentum and long-term political risk in France.
insights.quote: France is facing increasing problems with the cultural integration of young people born in France but who do not feel French
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha

insights.claim: Jérôme Fourquet and Ruben Rabinovitch argue in Homo Occidentalis that the West is undergoing 'décivilisation', a concept from Norbert Elias describing weakening self-control and growing licence for antisocial behaviour and violence.
insights.so_what: A structural decline in social cohesion would mean recurring unrest rather than one-off episodes.
insights.locator: There is perhaps yet another new
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha

insights.claim: Today's French riots are impulsive and ahistorical, lacking the utopian myths of 1789 and 1968, and the right increasingly describes such behaviour as 'ensauvagement' (society becoming feral).
insights.so_what: The spread of this framing signals that law-and-order politics favouring the right is gaining ground.
insights.quote: behaviours that are impulsive, ahistorical and unrelieved by the utopian myths of 1789 and 1968
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha

insights.claim: France's quasi-monarchical presidency and entrenched elites make reform hard to achieve through institutions, which sustains a tradition of direct action in the streets.
insights.so_what: Structural reform in France, such as pensions or the budget, faces recurring street resistance, a persistent risk premium.
insights.quote: makes reform very difficult to achieve, and that direct action, i.e. taking to the streets, is a better way to make your demands heard
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha

insights.claim: The 2018 gilets jaunes movement, a revolt of rural and peri-urban working and lower-middle classes against a green fuel tax, was framed as a modern jacquerie.
insights.so_what: Climate taxes that hit peripheral voters can trigger mass revolt, a lesson for energy-transition policy.
insights.locator: Since then, the memory of jacqueries
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha

insights.claim: In May 68, students (92% middle-class) and striking factory workers had different goals, with workers seeking pay and conditions rather than revolution, and the movement ended without a coup or civil war.
insights.so_what: Unrest becomes systemic only when it fuses with labour action, so watch whether unions join.
insights.speaker: Muriel Zagha
